Eradicate

/ehr-RAD-i-kayt/ — stress on second syllable, rhymes with 'dedicate' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To eradicate something is to destroy it so completely that none of it remains.

The campaign hopes to eradicate the invasive beetles within five years.

Worked Example

After the city discovered harmful bacteria in the water supply, officials launched an urgent mission to eradicate every trace of contamination.

Eradicate is more precise than 'eliminate' or 'destroy' because it specifically means complete destruction with nothing remaining. If you merely eliminate or remove something, traces might be left behind—but eradicate demands total annihilation.

How Strong Is It? — reduce → eliminate → obliterate → eradicate

reduce vs. eradicate

reduce vs. eradicate: Reduce is far weaker than eradicate; reduce only lessens the amount, while eradicate wipes something out so completely that none remains.

eliminate vs. eradicate

eliminate vs. eradicate: Eliminate is close to eradicate, but eradicate is more thorough — it means pulling something out by the roots so it cannot return.

obliterate vs. eradicate

obliterate vs. eradicate: Obliterate and eradicate both mean total destruction, but eradicate stresses removing every trace of an unwanted thing, while obliterate stresses blotting it out.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Root — -radic-: root (Latin)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: E- means 'out' and -radic- means 'root,' so to eradicate is literally to root something out — to destroy it so completely that nothing is left.

Use the root in a new word: radish

Use the root in a new word: radish: A radish is the swollen root of a plant, and eradicate literally means to pull something out by the roots.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / technical

Eradicate is precise when complete destruction is essential—when you need absolutely nothing to remain. Use it for disease-elimination campaigns, invasive species control, or problems that must be totally gone. For everyday destruction, 'destroy' is simpler and more common.
